8. The Enabler of Misconduct: Attorney Robert A. 
Giacovas 
The successful execution of Bleich's litigation strategy relies heavily on the selection of legal 
counsel willing to adopt a matching operational philosophy. Robert A. Giacovas possesses a 
deeply documented public history of identical misconduct, systemic professional delinquency, 
and judicial rebukes, making him the ideal architect for Bleich's extortionate maneuvers.1 
Systemic Professional Delinquency: New Jersey PHV Ineligibility 
Giacovas’s disregard for fundamental compliance rules extends to his own administrative 
licensing. According to the New Jersey Lawyers' Fund for Client Protection's 2025 Ineligible 
Lists, Robert Giacovas (Attorney ID PHV012046) is formally listed as ineligible to practice.1 The 
Supreme Court of New Jersey issued this order because Giacovas failed to comply with 
multijurisdictional practice regulations—specifically failing to pay the mandatory annual 
assessment ($267) and associated late fees for the 2025 cycle.1 Consequently, he was rendered 
ineligible to appear Pro Hac Vice in New Jersey effective June 30, 2025.1 This failure to maintain 
basic jurisdictional reporting requirements solidifies a pattern of systemic administrative 
delinquency.1 
The Medifast SLAPP Case: A Template for Malicious Litigation 
The tactics Giacovas deployed against Arnulf Damerau are a near-perfect replication of his 
misconduct in the federal litigation Medifast, Inc. v. Tracy Coenen, et al. (S.D. Cal. 
3:10-cv-00382).1 In that matter, Giacovas and co-counsel Lainie E. Cohen filed an aggressive 
$270 million defamation lawsuit against a forensic accountant.1 The litigation was ultimately 
categorized as a Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation (SLAPP)—a meritless action 
engineered specifically to silence, intimidate, and bankrupt critics through the crushing burden 
of legal defense costs.1 
Throughout the Medifast litigation, Giacovas was accused of systematically fabricating 
statements and affirmatively misleading the federal court to survive anti-SLAPP dismissal.1 In 
his pleadings, Giacovas falsely argued that the defendant explicitly accused his client of 
running a "Ponzi scheme" and committing "securities fraud".1 The presiding federal judge 
severely rebuked this tactic, ruling that Giacovas failed to plead exact words and instead 
"paraphrases Defendants' statements in its pleadings, seemingly for maximum shock value".1 
The court concluded that no reasonable factfinder could interpret the writings as a provably 
false assertion of a criminal scheme.1 
Furthermore, Giacovas was accused of malicious "scorched-earth" procedural tactics to 
maximize billable hours and inflate the defendant's legal expenses.1 For instance, immediately
